paragraphs: BrainFlow studies how the brain’s relatively fixed structural connections relate to changing patterns of functional connectivity across cognitive states. Direct mappings between structure and individual functional states can be inconsistent because different states share overlapping networks. The paper instead models how one structural connectivity pattern can connect to multiple functional patterns.

The method treats this relationship as a flow between distributions, conditioned on cognitive state. It constructs the flow on a curved mathematical space suited to symmetric positive-definite connectivity matrices. The authors prove an equivalence between flow matching in this space and in a computationally cheaper space based on Cholesky representations.

BrainFlow also introduces consensus control to coordinate pathways and encourage the shared structures present across cognitive states. Together, these components form a reversible generative model of structure–function relationships. The authors report state-of-the-art performance on synthetic data and neuroimaging datasets from UK Biobank and the Human Connectome Project. The contribution combines a more flexible account of multiple functional states with an efficient mathematical formulation.
neurips-2025-brainflow-a-holistic-pathwa.tldr: BrainFlow models brain structure–function relationships as reversible, state-conditioned flows that coordinate shared patterns across cognitive states.

paragraphs: CoDA generates coordinated body, hand, and object motion for manipulating articulated objects. These interactions require both broad postural adjustments and precise finger placement on movable parts. Treating hand motion separately from body motion makes it difficult to satisfy these interdependent requirements.

The framework optimizes the noise inputs of three specialized diffusion models: one for the body and one for each hand. Each model learns from its own motion dataset. Coordination comes through gradients that follow the human kinematic chain, allowing objectives for hand movement to influence the overall body posture.

For precise interaction, CoDA represents object geometry and hand end-effector positions using distances to a shared set of reference points. This captures detailed spatial relationships and supplies trajectory targets for noise optimization. The authors report better motion quality and physical plausibility than existing approaches. They also demonstrate object pose control, walking while manipulating objects, and generating whole-body motion from hand-only data. These results show how specialized motion models can be coordinated through shared optimization objectives.
neurips-2025-coda-coordinated-diffusion-.tldr: CoDA coordinates separate body and hand diffusion models through noise optimization to generate precise whole-body interactions with articulated objects.

paragraphs: Compress & Cache addresses the cost of representing images with many visual tokens in large vision-language models. Its goal is a compact representation that supports both language generation and discriminative tasks such as retrieval. Compression happens in an upfront indexing stage, separating that work from later generation.

Training uses two forward passes through the language model. The first compresses dense image tokens into a small collection of summary tokens. The second combines those summaries with language instructions, replacing the original visual tokens. An autoregressive objective trains the summaries to preserve information needed for generation, while a contrastive objective strengthens their usefulness for discriminative tasks.

The method also uses adapters specific to the two stages. The authors report twice the compression rate without compromising generative capabilities, alongside state-of-the-art image retrieval and compositionality results. Ablation studies support the effectiveness of the design. The central finding is that a shared compressed representation can serve both kinds of tasks when training explicitly accounts for their different requirements.
neurips-2025-compress-cache-vision-token.tldr: Compress & Cache learns reusable visual summaries that support generation and retrieval while moving compression into an upfront indexing stage.

paragraphs: This paper studies uncertainty estimation when a generative model is accessible only through a limited number of queries. The task is to build prediction sets that balance coverage, informativeness, and query cost. Conventional conformal methods use structured outputs or scores that do not directly fit this setting.

The proposed CPQ framework connects two design decisions to missing mass: the probability assigned to outputs that have not yet appeared in the sampled responses. The optimal query policy depends on how quickly this unseen probability decreases, for which the authors develop an estimator. The mapping from sampled responses to prediction sets depends on missing mass itself, estimated using Good-Turing methods.

This separates deciding how to query from deciding what prediction set to return, while linking both decisions through a common statistical quantity. Experiments cover three open-ended tasks and two language models. The authors report more informative prediction sets than existing conformal language-uncertainty methods and examine each principle’s contribution. The query-only formulation supports application to black-box language models.
neurips-2025-conformal-prediction-beyond.tldr: CPQ uses estimates of unseen output probability to balance query cost, coverage, and prediction-set informativeness for black-box generative models.

paragraphs: DecompNet aims to improve time-series forecasting using knowledge associated with decomposition, without requiring the forecasting model to decompose its input during inference. Its central idea is implicit decomposition: the model receives the benefit of decomposition-related knowledge even though explicit decomposition is absent from the prediction process.

This distinction matters because an enhancement can improve forecasting while also adding work whenever a prediction is made. DecompNet is designed to preserve the performance benefit without introducing additional inference costs. The contribution is presented as an enhancement framework for forecasting models, making its ability to improve different models an important part of the evaluation.

The authors report promising gains across models, including recent state-of-the-art forecasters, and describe broad framework generality. Their comparisons also show advantages in performance and efficiency over established normalization-based enhancement frameworks. These findings support implicit decomposition as a way to incorporate useful forecasting knowledge while retaining an efficient inference path. The reported generality concerns the models evaluated, rather than establishing that every possible forecasting model will improve.
neurips-2025-decompnet-enhancing-time-se.tldr: DecompNet improves forecasting by supplying decomposition-related knowledge without explicitly decomposing inputs or adding inference costs.

paragraphs: Diffusion models learn score functions at different noise levels to guide sample generation. This paper asks how many training samples are needed to learn those functions. Previous bounds depended polynomially on data dimension, beyond a separate term measuring the size of the candidate function class.

The authors establish nearly dimension-free sample complexity bounds, while retaining any dimensional dependence contained in that function-class term. A crucial feature is using one function approximator across noise levels, allowing information to transfer across timesteps. Their analysis introduces a martingale-based error decomposition and sharp variance bounds to handle dependent observations generated by Markov processes.

The paper also proposes Bootstrapped Score Matching, which uses scores already learned at earlier noise levels to reduce variance and improve accuracy at higher noise levels. The theoretical result helps explain why jointly learning across time can be statistically efficient. Its dimension-free description is qualified: complexity associated with the hypothesis class can still depend on dimension. The proposed training technique builds directly on the analysis of shared learning across noise levels.
neurips-2025-dimension-free-score-matchi.tldr: The paper proves nearly dimension-free score-learning bounds and proposes reusing learned scores to reduce variance across diffusion noise levels.

paragraphs: Bayesian experiment design chooses experiments adaptively as observations update beliefs about the unknown system. Deep learning can make these choices efficient, but training faces a growing coverage problem. As an experiment proceeds, the number of possible beliefs becomes enormous, requiring offline training to sample many different situations.

The authors call this difficulty belief explosion and argue that network architecture is central to addressing it. They focus on the inductive biases of actor and critic networks: the built-in structure that influences how these networks learn decisions and evaluate them. Their proposed approach uses graph neural networks with permutation equivariance suited to the experiment-design domain.

Permutation equivariance makes a network respond consistently when domain elements are reordered, letting its architecture reflect that symmetry. The authors report improvements of multiple orders of magnitude in sample efficiency compared with naive parameterizations. The result identifies a concrete route to reducing the training burden: encode relevant domain structure in the networks used for adaptive experimental decisions.
neurips-2025-efficient-bayesian-experime.tldr: Graph networks that respect domain permutations substantially reduce the training samples needed for learned Bayesian experiment design.

paragraphs: Estimating uncertainty in free-form answers requires comparing meanings, because differently worded responses can express the same answer. Repeatedly generating semantically redundant responses can make stable uncertainty estimates expensive. This paper proposes steering sampling toward a broader range of meanings to obtain more useful information from a fixed generation budget.

The sampler applies a continuous semantic-similarity penalty during decoding. A natural language inference model, lightly fine-tuned on partial outputs, supplies the semantic signal. The approach accommodates both autoregressive generation and masked diffusion. Because steering changes the sampling distribution, the method uses importance reweighting to debias uncertainty estimates and control variates to reduce their variance.

Across four question-answering benchmarks, the method matches or exceeds baseline performance while reaching more semantic clusters with the same number of samples. It requires no gradient access to the underlying language model. The findings support a modular approach to more efficient semantic uncertainty estimation, with statistical corrections allowing deliberate diversity in generation to remain useful for measuring uncertainty.
neurips-2025-efficient-semantic-uncertai.tldr: A diversity-steered sampler explores more answer meanings and statistically corrects its estimates to measure uncertainty with fewer redundant generations.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning and controlling linear systems that evolve continuously, even though an algorithm observes them only a finite number of times. The first task is system identification: estimating the parameters governing the system’s dynamics. The authors provide a non-asymptotic analysis, describing estimation error with finite observations.

Their estimator does not require observations integrated over time intervals. This removes a measurement requirement that the authors identify as an obstacle to practical use. They also prove a lower bound showing that the estimator’s error is optimal up to constant factors, giving a theoretical benchmark for its statistical efficiency.

The identification method then supports online control by enabling more efficient exploration and faster recognition of ineffective policies. For a controllable system over a single horizon of length T, the authors obtain regret growing as the square root of T using only order-T observations. This connects finite-observation parameter estimation to control performance, with controllability explicitly conditioning the stated control guarantee.
neurips-2025-finite-sample-analyses-for-.tldr: The paper gives optimal finite-observation system identification up to constants and uses it to obtain square-root-time regret in controllable continuous-time linear systems.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether reinforcement learning for mathematical problem solving also develops the ability to evaluate reasoning processes. Process reward models provide this kind of supervision explicitly. The authors find that problem-solving ability and process-evaluation capability develop together during pure reinforcement learning, making their relationship more nuanced than separate training roles suggest.

They also find that current process reward models perform worse than simple majority voting when used with strong reasoning models such as DeepSeek-R1 and QwQ-32B. To address this, they introduce Self-PRM, in which a model evaluates and reranks its own generated solutions through self-reward mechanisms.

Self-PRM consistently improves benchmark accuracy, especially when more candidate solutions are available. However, its precision on difficult problems remains below 10%, and it often accepts flawed solutions as valid. The results therefore support both emerging self-evaluation capability and a substantial reliability gap. The authors argue for combining process supervision with further reinforcement-learning scaling to improve reward alignment and introspective accuracy.
neurips-2025-is-prm-necessary-problem-so.tldr: Problem-solving reinforcement learning develops self-evaluation abilities, but Self-PRM’s accuracy gains coexist with poor precision on difficult problems.

paragraphs: ODG predicts which parts of a surrounding three-dimensional scene are occupied and what those regions contain, using camera images. Dense scene grids become difficult to scale to high resolution. A single collection of sparse queries, meanwhile, can struggle to represent objects with different characteristics.

The method separates driving scenes into static and dynamic components and assigns them dual sets of sparse Gaussian queries. A hierarchical Gaussian transformer predicts occupied voxel centers, semantic classes, and Gaussian parameters. This representation gives the model distinct ways to handle the different components while maintaining a sparse description of the scene.

ODG also uses 3D Gaussian Splatting to render predictions and compare them with available depth and semantic annotations. This adds pixel-level alignment signals to occupancy learning. Experiments on Occ3D-nuScenes and Occ3D-Waymo achieve state-of-the-art results while retaining low inference cost. The reported findings support combining a structured sparse representation with image-level supervision to improve detailed three-dimensional perception efficiently.
neurips-2025-odg-occupancy-prediction-us.tldr: ODG combines separate static and dynamic Gaussian representations with rendering supervision for accurate, low-cost 3D occupancy prediction.

paragraphs: This paper asks which architectural preferences help diffusion transformers generalize. Earlier work studied locally linear UNet denoisers through eigen-decompositions of their Jacobians. The nonlinear operations in transformer denoisers prevent the same analysis from revealing their inductive biases, motivating a different investigation centered on attention.

The authors find that local attention in early transformer layers is closely associated with generalization. They then restrict attention windows and observe improved generalization, providing an intervention beyond the initial association. Their experiments also show that the placement of these windows and their effective attention size are crucial.

Results on CelebA, ImageNet, MSCOCO, and LSUN show that strengthening this architectural preference can improve both generalization and image quality when training data is limited. The finding is specific about where the benefit comes from: local attention must be configured appropriately. It offers an empirical explanation and a design direction for diffusion transformers under reduced data availability, rather than establishing that every restriction on attention improves generation.
neurips-2025-on-inductive-biases-that-en.tldr: Appropriately placed local attention windows improve diffusion-transformer generalization and generation quality in experiments with limited training data.

paragraphs: Simple bilevel optimization minimizes an upper-level objective over solutions to a lower-level problem. This paper considers smooth objectives that can both be nonconvex. Without additional lower-level structure such as convexity or the Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition, finding a globally optimal solution is generally intractable.

The authors introduce a stationarity criterion suited to this setting. Intuitively, a point is stationary when the upper-level objective cannot be substantially improved locally without a larger deterioration in the lower-level objective. This creates a tractable target that accounts for both objectives and their unequal roles.

They show that an implementable variant of dynamic barrier gradient descent reaches this joint stationarity target in polynomial time. The complexity depends on separate accuracy requirements for the two levels and a nonnegative parameter that balances the terms. The authors describe this as the first such complexity guarantee for a discrete-time algorithm in general nonconvex simple bilevel optimization. The guarantee concerns approximate stationarity at both levels, rather than global optimization.
neurips-2025-on-the-complexity-of-findin.tldr: A dynamic barrier gradient method reaches a newly defined joint stationarity target in polynomial time for smooth nonconvex simple bilevel problems.

paragraphs: PairEdit learns an image-editing transformation from source–target image pairs without textual guidance. This addresses edits whose intended meaning is difficult to express precisely in words. The method can learn from a small number of pairs or even one pair, making the visual example itself the specification of the change.

The approach introduces a target noise prediction with a guidance-direction term that explicitly represents semantic differences between the paired images. A content-preserving noise schedule supports learning the intended change while retaining image content. Separate low-rank adaptation modules, or LoRAs, disentangle learning the semantic variation from learning the content.

These components address the distinction between what should change and what should remain consistent. Qualitative and quantitative evaluations show that PairEdit learns intricate editing semantics and significantly improves content consistency compared with baseline methods. The contribution is therefore both a text-free way to specify edits through examples and a mechanism for separating the desired transformation from the particular content of those examples.
neurips-2025-pairedit-learning-semantic-.tldr: PairEdit learns complex edits from as little as one image pair, using separate mechanisms for semantic change and content preservation without text guidance.

paragraphs: PanTS is a dataset for training and evaluating AI systems that analyze pancreatic CT scans. It contains 36,390 scans from 145 medical centers, with expert-validated labels for more than 993,000 anatomical structures. These labels identify structures at the voxel level, providing detailed three-dimensional outlines within each scan.

The annotations cover pancreatic tumors, the head, body, and tail of the pancreas, and 24 surrounding anatomical structures. Each scan also includes patient and imaging metadata, such as diagnosis, contrast phase, and slice thickness. This combines detailed tumor labels with anatomical context and information about how the images were acquired.

Models trained on PanTS perform significantly better at tumor detection, localization, and segmentation than models trained on existing public datasets. The authors attribute the gains directly to tumor annotations at 16 times the scale and indirectly to the surrounding-structure labels. PanTS therefore contributes both a larger training resource and a benchmark for studying how annotation scale and anatomical context improve pancreatic CT analysis.
neurips-2025-pants-the-pancreatic-tumor-.tldr: PanTS provides large-scale, detailed pancreatic CT annotations that improve reported tumor detection, localization, and segmentation performance.

paragraphs: Masked generative models create images through repeated decoding steps that use surrounding context. Decoding more tokens at once can reduce the number of steps, but it also treats those tokens independently at that step. This misses dependencies and can substantially reduce image fidelity.

ReCAP accelerates generation by making some steps cheaper while preserving fine-grained iteration. It alternates standard full model evaluations with lightweight steps that reuse cached feature embeddings from previously decoded context tokens. The approach reduces repeated computation while retaining the opportunity to incorporate context across successive generation steps.

The authors evaluate ReCAP with MaskGIT, MAGE, and MAR, covering different architectures and both discrete and continuous token representations. On class-conditional ImageNet256 generation, it achieves up to 2.4 times faster inference than the base model with minimal performance loss. Across generation settings, it delivers better efficiency–fidelity trade-offs. The results support feature reuse as a practical way to accelerate iterative masked generation without relying solely on decoding larger batches of tokens simultaneously.
neurips-2025-plug-and-play-context-featu.tldr: ReCAP reuses cached context features between full evaluations to speed up masked image generation with minimal reported fidelity loss.

paragraphs: Diffusion inversion seeks a generative trajectory that reconstructs a given real image. Accurate inversion matters for editing because it helps preserve consistency with the original image. Existing fixed-point formulations face difficulties balancing accuracy and efficiency, especially for few-step models and unfamiliar samples.

PreciseInv reformulates inversion as a learning problem solved through test-time optimization. A strategy inspired by dynamic programming recursively estimates a parameterized sequence of noise embeddings. It uses the smoothness of diffusion latent space for gradient-based optimization, while recursive subproblems support memory efficiency. The authors also analyze convergence and establish an upper bound on reconstruction error.

The framework enables faithful inversion with as few as two inference steps. Experiments on COCO 2017, DarkFace, and stylized cartoons report state-of-the-art reconstruction quality and inference speed, with especially notable gains for few-step models and distribution shifts. More precise reconstruction also improves consistency in text-guided editing. These findings connect better recovery of the original image’s generative trajectory to more reliable subsequent manipulation.
neurips-2025-precise-diffusion-inversion.tldr: PreciseInv learns noise trajectories through recursive test-time optimization, improving diffusion inversion speed, reconstruction, and editing consistency.

paragraphs: This paper studies releasing running totals with differential privacy when the stream’s final length is unknown. Strong existing matrix-based methods need parameters tuned to that length for their privacy guarantees. The common doubling approach avoids knowing it beforehand, but introduces suboptimal error that changes unevenly.

The authors construct new matrix factorizations using logarithmic perturbations of a function studied in earlier work. Their algorithm produces smooth error growth and estimates the sum through time t with variance O(log^(2+2α)(t)) for any positive α. It uses O(t) space and amortized O(log t) processing time per round.

The comparison is with a nearly optimal bounded-input method that requires O(n) space and O(n log n) preprocessing, where n is the known final length. Empirically, the new method’s variance stays below 1.5 times that method’s variance for t as large as 2^24. This shows that accommodating an unknown horizon can retain competitive practical error while supporting incremental processing without advance knowledge of the eventual stream size.
neurips-2025-private-continual-counting-.tldr: A new private running-total algorithm handles unknown stream lengths with smooth error, logarithmic amortized updates, and competitive empirical variance.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether the internal mechanisms behind language-model refusals are shared across languages. Prior work found that a single direction in activation space can mediate refusal behavior, mainly in English-focused settings. The authors investigate the multilingual case using PolyRefuse, a dataset of malicious and benign English prompts translated into 14 languages.

They find that a refusal direction extracted from English can bypass refusals in other languages with near-perfect effectiveness and without additional fine-tuning. They also report transfer between directions derived from other safety-aligned languages. This suggests that the studied models share a closely related internal refusal mechanism across their aligned languages.

The authors attribute this transfer to refusal vectors being parallel across languages in the model’s representation space. That geometric relationship provides an explanation for the cross-language behavior observed in their study. The findings expose a multilingual safety vulnerability and offer a mechanistic basis for developing stronger defenses. The empirical scope remains the investigated languages and models, despite the broad transfer reported within that setting.
neurips-2025-refusal-direction-is-univer.tldr: Across 14 studied languages, refusal directions transfer strongly between safety-aligned languages, revealing a shared multilingual safety vulnerability.

paragraphs: SCONE expands a language model’s input representations using embeddings for frequent sequences of tokens, or n-grams. It keeps the original vocabulary, avoiding an increase in decoding costs from vocabulary expansion. The additional embeddings provide each input token with a representation informed by its surrounding token sequence.

A separate model learns these contextualized embeddings during training. Afterward, they are precomputed and stored outside accelerator memory. Inference retrieves them through low-complexity lookups, which the authors report have minimal latency impact. This allows scaling either the number of stored n-gram embeddings or the model that learns them while keeping inference accelerator FLOPS and memory fixed.

The authors show that scaling both components lets a model with one billion accelerator-resident parameters outperform a 1.9-billion-parameter baseline across diverse corpora. It uses about half the inference FLOPS and accelerator memory. The result demonstrates a way to improve language-model performance by moving representational capacity into precomputed, externally stored embeddings rather than requiring all additional capacity to occupy the accelerator during inference.
neurips-2025-scaling-embedding-layers-in.tldr: SCONE scales contextual n-gram embeddings stored off accelerator to improve language-model performance while keeping inference accelerator usage fixed.

paragraphs: ShoeFit addresses virtual footwear try-on: generating an image of a person wearing specified shoes while preserving shape, texture, and color. The paper identifies three difficulties: scarce matched training data, mismatched viewpoints between product images and feet, and color distortion caused by environmental lighting interacting with footwear materials.

The authors introduce MVShoes, a dataset of 7,305 annotated image triplets spanning footwear categories and challenging scenarios. Their ShoeFit model uses a dual-stream diffusion transformer. Multi-view conditioning with three-dimensional rotary position embeddings addresses viewpoint mismatch, while LayeredRefAttention uses background features to modulate footwear representations and reduce environmental distortion.

Separate denoising and conditioning branches help preserve texture while disentangling shoe appearance from environmental interference. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations report substantial improvements in rendering fidelity and robustness for challenging real-world product shoes. The contribution combines task-specific data with architectural mechanisms aimed at distinct sources of visual error. The abstract states that the dataset and benchmark will become publicly available upon paper acceptance.
neurips-2025-shoefit-a-new-dataset-and-d.tldr: ShoeFit pairs a multi-view footwear dataset with a dual-stream diffusion transformer to improve viewpoint alignment, texture preservation, and color fidelity.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to represent and evaluate spatial reasoning in foundation models using driving scenes. Textual prompts and question-answer scoring can obscure geometry and allow linguistic shortcuts. The authors introduce Spatial Intelligence Grid, or SIG, as a structured representation that makes scene layout and spatial relationships explicit.

SIG encodes object positions, relations between objects, and physically grounded priors in a grid-based schema that complements text. The authors also derive evaluation metrics intended to distinguish spatial capability from language priors. This gives both the model inputs and the evaluation a direct connection to the represented scene structure.

In few-shot in-context learning experiments with multimodal language models, SIG produces larger and more stable improvements across the reported spatial metrics than VQA-only representations. The paper also introduces SIGBench, containing 1,400 driving frames with ground-truth SIG annotations and human gaze traces. Together, these resources support grid-based spatial tasks and attention-oriented tasks, while the experimental gains suggest SIG’s promise as a labeling and training format.
neurips-2025-towards-physics-informed-sp.tldr: SIG explicitly represents driving-scene geometry and improves measured spatial reasoning in few-shot experiments, supported by a new annotated benchmark.

paragraphs: The neural tangent kernel describes aspects of a neural network’s training behavior and changes in ways associated with feature learning. At the edge of stability, its largest eigenvalue oscillates around a value inversely related to the gradient-descent step size. Previous investigations examined this eigenvalue behavior more closely than the associated eigenvectors.

This paper focuses on how those eigenvectors evolve. Across different architectures, the authors observe that larger learning rates produce final kernels whose leading eigenvectors align more strongly with the training target. They also find greater target alignment for the full kernel matrix, extending the observation beyond its leading directions.

The authors investigate the mechanism and provide a theoretical analysis for a two-layer linear network. This distinguishes the broader empirical observations from the specific setting covered by the theory. The contribution is a more directional account of learning dynamics: learning rate is associated not only with the magnitude of kernel eigenvalues, but also with how the kernel’s dominant directions relate to the target being learned.
neurips-2025-understanding-the-evolution.tldr: Larger learning rates are empirically associated with stronger target alignment of neural tangent kernels, with a mechanism analyzed in a two-layer linear network.

paragraphs: UtilGen generates synthetic training data according to its usefulness for a downstream task. Visually realistic and diverse images may not satisfy the specific needs of every task or network architecture. The framework therefore uses feedback from the downstream task to guide what the generator produces.

A weight allocation network estimates the task-specific utility of each synthetic sample. Those evaluations drive two forms of adaptation. Model-level optimization adjusts the generator to the task, while instance-level optimization changes generation choices, including prompt embeddings and initial noise, at each round. This creates an iterative process in which assessed usefulness informs subsequent data generation.

Experiments on eight benchmark datasets report consistently superior performance and an average accuracy improvement of 3.87% over previous state-of-the-art methods. Further analyses of data influence and distribution indicate that the generated samples are more impactful and task-relevant. The findings support judging synthetic data through its contribution to downstream learning, alongside adapting both the generator itself and the choices used to produce individual samples.
neurips-2025-utilgen-utility-centric-gen.tldr: UtilGen uses downstream feedback to adapt both a generator and its per-sample choices, producing synthetic data with greater reported training utility.

paragraphs: This paper investigates when in-context learning can benefit from demonstrations with missing labels. Its theory studies a binary Gaussian mixture model with partially labeled examples. In this setting, one-layer linear attention recovers the optimal fully supervised estimator but fails to make use of the unlabeled data.

Multilayer or looped transformers can exploit unlabeled examples by implicitly constructing polynomial estimators from the features and observed labels. The authors characterize which polynomials different depths can express and connect the mechanism to expectation maximization, an iterative pseudo-labeling method. The leading polynomial power grows exponentially with depth, so a modest amount of depth or looping can suffice.

The authors apply this insight by looping existing tabular foundation models to strengthen their semi-supervised learning capability. Evaluations on real-world datasets show significant improvements over ordinary single-pass inference. The theoretical conclusion is tied to the stated mixture-model setting, while the tabular experiments demonstrate a practical use of the depth-and-iteration mechanism beyond that theoretical analysis.
neurips-2025-when-and-how-unlabeled-data.tldr: Theory explains how transformer depth or looping enables use of unlabeled demonstrations, motivating improved semi-supervised inference for tabular foundation models.
